chunks: A number of our companions, from Ahmad ibn Muhammad, from Ibn Mahboub, from Abu Ayoub al-Khazzaz, from Abu Abdillah (peace be upon him), who said:

The man should seek permission when he enters upon his father, and the father does not seek permission from the son. He said: And the man should seek permission from his daughter and his sister when they are married.
ai.seo_question: What is the Islamic ruling on seeking permission to enter the private chambers of one's father, daughter, or sister?
ai.summary: This hadith from al-Kafi delineates the hierarchical etiquette of privacy (istid'ān) within the family, emphasizing that while a son must seek permission from his father, the reverse is not required, reflecting the father's authority. It further extends this requirement to married daughters and sisters, highlighting that marriage establishes a distinct private sphere for women, necessitating formal permission even from their fathers or brothers. This ruling underscores the balance between familial closeness and the preservation of individual modesty in Shia jurisprudence.

en.hubeali:
A number of our companions, from Ahmad Bin Muhammad, from Ibn Mahboub, from Abu Ayoub Al Khazzaz, 
(It has been narrated) from Abu Abdullah<sup>asws</sup> having said: ‘

The man should seek permission when he enters the (chambers of) his father, but the father shall not seek permission from the son; and the man shall seek permission of his daughter and his sister when they were married (before entering into their chambers)’.
en.sarwar: 3. Ahmad ibn Muhammad has narrated from ibn Faddal from abu Jamilah from Muhammad ibn Ali al-Halabiy who has said the following: “I once asked abu ‘Abd Allah, ‘Alayhi al-Salam, if a man is required to ask permission from his father.

He (the Imam) said, ‘Yes, I would ask permission from my father and my mother was not with him. She was my father’s wife. My mother had died when I was a boy. I did not like to disturb their privacy and they also did not like it. It is very correct and fine to say Salam (the phrase of offering greeting of peace).”’
